activities.anchor: how sources are chosen, used and doubted
activities.caption: file the figure-drawing sources
activities.name: figSrcSort

config.prompt: The figure is learned from sources — file each one:

items.label: the life model — three-dimensional, breathing, imperfect
master copies — drawing after Michelangelo, Rubens, Ingres
anatomy plates — Richer, Bridgman, Goldfinger, Peck
sculpture in museums — the cast collection

config.why: The primary source trains seeing — weight shifts teach balance, foreshortening teaches space; the secondary sources supply accumulated solutions. The AO1 discipline is selecting and using both deliberately, with the intention stated.

activities.anchor: drawn long, fast and from the shoulder
activities.caption: a timed pose session, in duration order
activities.name: figSessOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the timed session — each duration adds a decision layer:
items: 30-second poses — pure gesture: the line of action, the pose's intent
config.why: Each duration trains a different decision speed, and the compounding of years of weekly sessions is the actual mechanism by which the skill arrives — there is no shortcut, only distribution of practice.

activities.anchor: trace the silhouette and fill it in
activities.caption: one step of this beginner's method is wrong
activities.name: figContourSpot

config.prompt: One step of this beginner's method is wrong — click it:
lines: Start with a few long, fast lines capturing the pose's dominant curve.
Lay down the figure's outline first, then work inward from it.
Draw C- and S-curves running through the limbs, from the shoulder.
Hang the structure on the living action, never the reverse.
Find the edges as consequences of the structure you laid down.
config.correction: The outline records only where the figure's edge happened to be and says nothing about the action that put it there — the action line goes down before any edge, and a hundred hours of contour practice produce figures that look traced and dead.
config.why: Contour is the slowest, least informative thing to draw first; gesture-first reverses the dependency so structure hangs on a living action and the edges are found as consequences.

activities.caption: place the eyes on the head's vertical scale
activities.name: figEyesPlace

config.prompt: Beginners draw the eyes a third of the way down from the top. Place them where they actually sit on the head:
config.why: The face divides at the eyes — they sit at the vertical midpoint of the head, a fact beginners disbelieve weekly; the nose then sits halfway between eyes and chin, the mouth a third below the nose.

activities.caption: muscle by function, mass by metaphor
activities.name: figMuscleMatch

config.prompt: Match each structure to how the artist uses it:

pairs.right: drawn as an egg — the upper armature mass
drawn as a bucket or box — the lower armature mass
flexes the elbow — it bulges when working, flattens when stretched

config.why: Action-based knowledge predicts what a muscle does in a pose, where name-lists evaporate; the armature masses stay fixed to bone so landmarks do not drift with the flesh.

activities.caption: the slavish copy vs the copy with intention
activities.name: figCopyCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to copy a master drawing — drag the divider:

before.label: the slavish copy
before.text: replicates every line for its own sake — a facsimile in which the studied problem is never named and nothing transferable is taken away

after.label: the copy as conversation
after.text: the intention is stated — how Michelangelo compressed an arm, how Ingres directed a line — each copy reverse-engineers one solved problem

config.why: The atelier treats the copy as a conversation with the intention declared, so secondary sources supply accumulated solutions rather than imitation practice.

activities.caption: the flying gallop — what do you do with the photographs?
activities.name: figGallopBranch

config.root: It is 1878. Your academy has painted the flying gallop for centuries — forelegs flung forward, hind legs stretched back — and Muybridge's banked tripline cameras have just published. How do you treat the new source?

start.text: The photographs disagree with every inherited painting of the gallop. What now?

choices.label: Keep the flying gallop — tradition outranks apparatus
choices.feedback: Inherited convention just lost: observation outranks it — but note what the photographs cannot do either.

choices.label: Copy the photograph exactly — the shutter saw the truth
choices.feedback: Half right: the pictures corrected centuries of confident drawing almost overnight — yet a photograph is itself an instrument with opinions.

choices.label: Interrogate both — the eye reads the whole stride, the shutter chose one instant
choices.feedback: The atelier's conclusion: sources are interrogated, not obeyed — on either side.

tradition.text: You have kept an image no unaided eye ever caught and no tradition had earned — the exact failure the photographs exposed.

obey.text: Blindly copied photographs produce their own stiffness — lens foreshortening flattens faces and freezes balance the living eye reads continuously.

interrogate.text: The gallop photographs correct the tradition, and structural knowledge corrects the photograph — observation and instrument check each other.

config.why: Muybridge's 1878 pictures showed the horse gathering all four hooves beneath its body at once — a moment no unaided eye could catch — while remaining an instrument whose shutter chose the instant.

activities.caption: why hands and heads are hard
activities.name: figFamiliarCloze

config.text: Hands and heads are hard because they are %%0%% — every viewer is an %%1%% in them — so the fix is %%2%%: the hand as palm block plus rhythmic segments, the head as ball plus planes built on bony landmarks.
config.hint: Not 'complicated' — the difficulty comes from a lifetime of looking.
